description: Large, robust branching coral that forms thick, flattened branches resembling elk antlers. One of the most important reef-building corals in the Caribbean, providing critical habitat for fish and other marine life. Historically dominant on USVI shallow reefs before major declines.
habitat: Shallow reef zones, typically 1-5 meters depth, high-energy wave zones
identificationTips: Thick, broad branches that flatten toward the tips
Usually tan to golden-brown when healthy
Forms large colonies that can dominate shallow reefs
Most common in depths less than 5 meters
usviNotes: Heavily impacted by white band disease and hurricanes. Major restoration focus species.

description: Fast-growing branching coral with cylindrical branches resembling deer antlers. Forms dense thickets that provide important shelter for juvenile fish and invertebrates. Critical restoration species in USVI waters.
habitat: Mid-depth reef zones, typically 5-15 meters, protected areas with moderate water flow
identificationTips: Branches extend upward at various angles
Pale brown to tan when healthy
usviNotes: Active restoration efforts throughout USVI. Slower recovery than Elkhorn.

description: Common, hardy coral that forms dome-shaped or encrusting colonies. One of the most resilient Caribbean corals and now one of the most abundant species on USVI reefs after decline of other species. Very stress-tolerant.
habitat: Very adaptable, found from shallow to deep reefs, 1-40 meters
identificationTips: Tiny, closely-packed polyps (hard to see individual ones)
Often forms small domes or encrusting plates
usviNotes: Most common coral on modern USVI reefs. Fast-growing and stress-tolerant.
threatFactors: Generally resilient, but affected by extreme bleaching events

description: Plating coral forming thin, leaf-like structures. One of the most common corals on current USVI reefs. Forms extensive colonies in various growth patterns from flat plates to more complex structures.
habitat: Wide depth range, 1-40 meters, particularly common on reef slopes
identificationTips: Thin, plate-like or leaf-like growth forms
Can be purple, brown, or tan
Polyps in neat rows along ridges
usviNotes: Second most common coral species in recent USVI surveys.

description: Hardy, massive coral forming large boulder-shaped colonies. Very stress-tolerant and resistant to disease. One of the most common corals remaining on USVI reefs due to resilience.
habitat: Wide range of habitats, shallow to deep, 1-40 meters
identificationTips: Surface covered with small star-shaped corallites
usviNotes: Third most common species. Highly stress-tolerant.

photoAttribution.photographer: FWC Fish and Wildlife Research Institute

description: Large, massive coral with distinctive meandering valleys and ridges that resemble a brain. Long-lived and slow-growing, these corals can be several hundred years old. Important reef structure provider.
habitat: Found across reef zones, from shallow to deep, 3-30 meters depth
identificationTips: Wide valleys with thick, rounded ridges
usviNotes: Heavily affected by stony coral tissue loss disease.

photoAttribution.photographer: FWC Fish and Wildlife Research Institute

description: One of the most important reef-building corals in the Caribbean. Forms large, mountainous colonies with tall bumps and columns. Historically dominant species, now in decline. Slow-growing and long-lived.
habitat: Common on reef slopes and walls, 3-30 meters depth
identificationTips: Forms tall columns or mountainous bumps
Surface covered with small star-shaped corallites
usviNotes: Formerly most abundant coral on many USVI reefs. Severely impacted by disease.

description: Important reef-building coral forming large columns and lobes. Part of the Orbicella complex that historically dominated Caribbean reefs. Forms distinct pillar-like structures.
identificationTips: More regular column formation than O. faveolata
usviNotes: Part of Orbicella complex. Historically abundant, now declining.

description: Third species in the important Orbicella complex. Forms more massive, boulder-like colonies compared to its relatives. Important reef builder.
identificationTips: More rounded overall shape than other Orbicella
usviNotes: Part of declining Orbicella complex. Important historical reef builder.

description: Large, massive coral with distinctive large, widely-spaced polyps. One of the most common large corals on USVI reefs. Very recognizable due to large polyp size.
habitat: Wide range from shallow to deep, 3-80 meters
identificationTips: Large, prominent polyps (golf-ball sized when extended)
Widely spaced compared to other star corals
Often brown with green or yellow polyp centers
usviNotes: Common and relatively stable species in USVI.

description: Brain coral with narrow, tightly-packed meandering valleys. More regular and symmetrical pattern than other brain corals. Common on USVI reefs.
usviNotes: Susceptible to stony coral tissue loss disease.

description: Brain coral with deep, well-defined grooves between ridges. Distinctive angular appearance. Common throughout Caribbean including USVI.
identificationTips: More angular pattern than other brain corals
usviNotes: Affected by disease but more resilient than some species.

description: Branching coral forming thick finger-like structures. Member of hardy Porites genus. Common in USVI, especially in sheltered areas.
habitat: Shallow to mid-depth, 1-20 meters, often in protected bays
identificationTips: Branches can be short and stubby or longer
usviNotes: Hardy Porites species, common in bays and protected areas.

description: Smaller cousin of Massive Starlet Coral. Forms smaller colonies and can tolerate more extreme conditions. Very hardy and stress-tolerant.
habitat: Wide range including extreme environments, 0-40 meters
usviNotes: Very hardy, found in a variety of habitats including tide pools.

photoAttribution.photographer: FWC Fish and Wildlife Research Institute

description: Distinctive coral with large, smooth, flower-like polyps. Forms small branching colonies. Relatively uncommon but distinctive when found.

photoAttribution.photographer: FWC Fish and Wildlife Research Institute

description: Unique coral forming tall, thick columns. The only Caribbean coral with this distinctive pillar-like growth form. Critically endangered and rare.
habitat: Reef slopes and sand channels, 1-25 meters
identificationTips: Only coral with this growth form
usviNotes: Very rare in USVI. Critically endangered throughout range.

description: Small coral with distinctive elliptical corallites. Often forms small mounds. Recognizable by the elongated shape of individual polyps.

photoAttribution.photographer: FWC Fish and Wildlife Research Institute

description: Small to medium coral with distinctive star-shaped corallites that often have pink or purple coloration, giving it the 'blushing' name. Forms encrusting to mound shapes.
habitat: Wide range of depths and habitats, 1-60 meters
identificationTips: Often has pinkish or purplish tint

photoAttribution.photographer: FWC Fish and Wildlife Research Institute
